title: How a neuron learns
blurb: Draw a line to tell cats from dogs — then watch a real neuron tune its own line until it beats you.
objectives: What a neuron really is — a line that splits things into two groups
Why a line you draw by hand can't quite catch everything
How a neuron fixes its own line by learning from its mistakes
How to train one yourself, from scratch, on brand-new data

glossary.def: The tiniest part of an AI brain. With two clues it makes one call: this group or that one — by drawing a line.
The line a neuron draws. Everything on one side is one group; everything on the other side is the other.
The numbers that tilt and slide the line. Changing the weights moves the boundary.
Doing the same thing over and over: check which dots are on the wrong side, nudge the line a little, repeat.
How many it got on the right side, out of all of them. 100% means every dot is sorted correctly.

steps.title: A robot that sorts pets
steps.body:
Imagine a robot with one job: look at a pet and say **cat or dog**. It can't see fur or hear barks — all it gets is two clues: **how big the ears are** and **how long the tail is**.

If we put every pet on a chart — ear size going across, tail length going up — cats land in one corner and dogs in another. So here's the robot's whole trick: **draw a line** with cats on one side and dogs on the other. That line is the entire brain. Let's build it.

steps.title: First, a guess
steps.prompt: Do you think **one straight line** could separate almost all the cats from the dogs on that chart?
choices: Yes — one straight line could split most of them
No — you'd need a curvy, wiggly line
steps.afterPick: Hold that thought. You're about to draw the line yourself and see what really happens. →

steps.title: Draw the line yourself
steps.body: Here's the chart. **Drag the two purple dots** up and down to swing the line until cats and dogs are on different sides. Watch the **wrong** counter — get it as low as you can, then press **Lock in my line**.
steps.youWillDo: drag the line to split cats from dogs

steps.title: So close — but not perfect
steps.body:
Notice what happened: you got *most* of them, but a few stubborn dots stayed on the wrong side no matter how you tilted the line. That's not your fault — the groups overlap a little, and a line placed **by hand** can only do so much.

So here's the real question: how could the robot do **better** than your best guess? The secret is that it doesn't guess just once. It **adjusts** — again and again. Let's watch.

steps.title: Watch the neuron learn
steps.body: This line starts out **bad on purpose**. Press **Watch it learn**. Every time a dot is on the wrong side (it flashes with a red ring), the neuron **nudges the line a tiny bit** to fix it — then checks again, and again. Watch the wrong rings disappear.
steps.youWillDo: watch a neuron tune its own line

steps.title: Now it has names
steps.body:
What you just watched has real names — and now they'll make sense:

- The line is the **decision boundary**.
- The numbers that tilt and slide it are the neuron's **weights**.
- **Learning** is just this: after each mistake, nudge the weights a little so the line fits better — over and over.

That's it. That self-fixing loop *is* a neuron learning. Every AI you've heard of does this — only with a lot more dots and a lot more lines.

steps.title: Check yourself
steps.question: When the neuron "learns," what is actually changing each round?
choices: It deletes the dots it keeps getting wrong
Its weights — the numbers that tilt the line
steps.explain: Right! Learning = nudging the **weights** after each mistake. The dots never change — the line does.

steps.title: Your turn — train one
steps.body: New pets, and this time **no hints**. Set a rough line with the purple dots, then press **Train my neuron** and watch it finish the job on its own.
steps.youWillDo: train your own neuron on fresh data

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.prompt: In your own words: **how does a neuron learn** to tell two groups apart?
steps.placeholder: Like: it starts with a not-great line, then…

recall.question: A neuron starts with a line that isn't great. How does it get better?
choices: It nudges its weights a little after each mistake, over and over
It throws away the dots it gets wrong
It waits for a human to fix the line
recall.explain: Exactly — guess, see what's wrong, nudge the weights, repeat. That loop is the heartbeat of every AI.

steps.youWillDo: explain it back in your own words

steps.title: Same idea, gigantic scale 🎉
steps.body:
You just built and trained a real neuron — drew its boundary, watched it fix its own weights, then trained a fresh one solo. That exact loop, with **billions** of weights and millions of dots, is what powers the chatbots and image apps you've heard about.

One last thing: a single neuron can only draw **one straight line**. Some groups can't be split that way — they need a *curve*. The fix is to wire **many** neurons together into a **network**, and their simple lines combine into curves.

**Next up:** see this same idea make *words* — train a tiny language model in **How AI writes**.
